extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of constitutional law/political theory and educated general readers interested in British government
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and normative standards for judging the role, utility, and dangers of a constitutional (British-style) monarchy, especially its influence on appointment, continuance, and ending of ministries. The text weighs benefits (selection, experience, warning) against harms (prejudice, court influence, undue secrecy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy / mystery of the Crown
rubrics_metrics.description: That secrecy is, however, essential to the utility of English royalty as it now is. Above all things our royalty is to be reverenced... The mystery of the constitution... is its life. We must not let in daylight upon magic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that the Crown's secret prerogatives and mystique create reverence; exposing or probing the monarch (e.g., select committees) would destroy that reverence and reduce the sovereign to a mere combatant in politics. Use this criterion to weigh transparency against the sociopolitical value of mystique; anti-pattern: institutionalising inquiries that 'poke about' the monarchy and thereby politicise it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish formal routine duties from real sovereign authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Queen has to assent to and sign countless formal documents, which contain no matter of policy... These labours of routine may be dismissed from the discussion. It is not by them that the sovereign acquires his authority either for evil or for good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the monarch's importance, exclude purely ceremonial or clerical acts (signing commissions, routine documents) because they neither confer nor constitute political authority. Example: backlog of military commissions under George III shows such formal work is slavish labour and not political influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the monarch's role at three stages of government
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole course of a representative government has three stages — first, when a ministry is appointed; next, during its continuance; last, when it ends. Let us consider what is the exact use of the Queen at each of these stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite framework (appointment, continuance, ending) to analyze any monarch's constitutional function. The text systematically assesses how the sovereign can help or harm at each stage—e.g., selection of a premier at appointment; counsel/warning during continuance; influence on resignation/dismissal at ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarch as selector of ministers when parties are divided
rubrics_metrics.description: In the royal form of cabinet government the sovereign then has sometimes a substantial selection; if the constitutional monarch be a man of singular discernment... he may pick out from the ranks of the divided party its very best leader, even at a time when the party would not nominate him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value the monarch's capacity to act as an impartial, discerning selector in moments of party division (three-party situations or when predominant party is divided). Positive example: Prince Albert's influence; negative/contrast: George III's failures. This is a conditional benefit—dependent on the monarch's personal discernment and disinterest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk from monarch's prejudice or limited ability
rubrics_metrics.description: If the monarch be not so exempt from prejudice, and have not this nearly miraculous discernment, it is not likely that he will be able to make a wiser choice than the choice of the party itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the danger that hereditary monarchs tend to be 'ordinary men of restricted experience' whose prejudices (e.g., George III's antipathies) can distort appointments and policy. Treat claims of royal wisdom skeptically; look for empirical signs of bias or preference for mediocrity as a negative indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary (House-based) selection can substitute for Crown selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose the House of Commons — existing alone and by itself— to appoint the premier quite simply... let any member or members have the right of nominating a successor; after a proper interval... let the members present vote... the candidate with the greatest number be premier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a baseline test: imagine government without a sovereign and evaluate whether the Commons/cabinet system can produce stable ministers. The passage argues a parliament-alone method would largely replicate current outcomes, with party organisation dominating choice; this is an argument for the imitability of cabinet government without monarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premier must pass public parliamentary tests
rubrics_metrics.description: A prime minister must show what he is. He must meet the House of Commons in debate; he must be able to guide that assembly in the management of its business, to gain its ear in every emergency, to rule it in its hours of excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a candidate for premiership (or the value of selection methods), emphasize public-facing competencies: debating, guiding business, commanding confidence. Contrast with presidential systems where a weak candidate may hide behind ministers; in parliamentary systems the leader is exposed and accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-party instability requires moderation and coalition-building
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of three parties ... a satisfactory choice is impossible. The numerically weakest has the casting vote... A choice based on such self-denial can never be a firm choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In multi-party contexts evaluate whether moderate forces can combine to support a steady government; the monarch may help by selecting a minister acceptable to moderates, but long-term stability requires parties' self-denial and coalition-building (example: Lord Palmerston maintained government by a moderate coalition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign's constitutional rights: to be consulted, to encourage, to warn
rubrics_metrics.description: To state the matter shortly, the sovereign has, under a constitutional monarchy such as ours, three rights — the right to be consulted, the right to encourage, the right to warn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these three soft powers as the legitimate limit of sovereign intervention. Used discreetly by a wise monarch they can influence ministers without usurping responsibility. Examples: royal memorandum about keeping the Crown informed; warning can trouble a minister's mind and change policy without direct coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarch's accumulated experience is a political asset
rubrics_metrics.description: In the course of a long reign a sagacious king would acquire an experience with which few ministers could contend... He would have the advantage which a permanent under-secretary has over his parliamentary superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the monarch's long-term memory and continuity as useful for advising ministers and preventing repeated policy errors; use concrete historical references (King Leopold, Prince Albert, George III) to assess whether the monarch's experience has been a constructive influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of court influence and favoritism
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is no court there can be no evil influence from a court... Everybody knows to what sort of influences several Italian changes of government since the unity of Italy have been attributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising a monarchy, check for informal networks of influence (mistresses, favourites, courtiers) that can distort policy, especially during party division. Anti-patterns: vigorous court intrigue, ministerial appointments shaped by personal favour rather than merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarch must not displace parliamentary responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The royal form of ministerial government is the worst of all forms if it erect the subsidiary apparatus into the principal force, if it induce the assembly which ought to perform paramount duties to expect some one else to perform them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a normative constraint: a monarchy is harmful if it causes Parliament to abdicate responsibility. Evaluate institutional incentives—do parliamentary actors rely on the Crown to find governments? If so, the royal form is defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private audience deference impairs frank ministerial argument
rubrics_metrics.description: A conference between a minister and his sovereign can never be a conference of pure argument... A minister cannot make his own points as well when he knows that the king would not like to hear them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the informational/psychological costs of private royal audiences: physical/social deference (examples: Lord Chatham kneeling) tends to blunt ministers' candour and argumentative force. This is a structural drawback to relying on private royal influence rather than public parliamentary scrutiny.
